claims.text: Greg LaVecchia (Bloom Nutrition founder) asserts that making a late decision — delayed because you are waiting for perfection — is often more dangerous than making a fast, imperfect decision and improving in real time. The risk of slow movement compounds invisibly while the risk of a fast imperfect decision is visible and correctable.
claims.speaker: Greg LaVecchia
claims.mechanism: A late decision forfeits the feedback and iteration cycles that only begin after committing; a fast imperfect decision generates real-time data that enables course-correction, so the fast path accumulates more learning per unit time.

claims.text: Greg LaVecchia observes that after experiencing a few mistakes, most founders become obsessed with certainty: they overthink decisions, wait for perfect timing, and attempt to eliminate every possible risk before their next move. This obsession with certainty is where progress and entrepreneurship die.
claims.speaker: Greg LaVecchia
conditions: founder who has experienced prior business failures or costly mistakes
claims.mechanism: Prior painful mistakes condition founders to treat uncertainty as the enemy; the resulting certainty-seeking behavior halts action, which prevents any new feedback that would resolve the uncertainty — a self-reinforcing stall.

claims.text: Greg LaVecchia (Bloom Nutrition) reframes past catastrophic-feeling mistakes as among the cheapest lessons he could have bought. What felt like world-ending errors at the time proved to be low-cost learning experiences in retrospect, suggesting the emotional magnitude of a mistake at the time of occurrence systematically overstates its actual cost.
claims.speaker: Greg LaVecchia
conditions: survivable business mistakes (not existential solvency failures)
claims.mechanism: Perceived catastrophe triggers disproportionate fear response; once survived, the mistake resolves into a bounded lesson with a concrete cost — making the fear revealed as inflated relative to the actual consequence.
bounded_by: Does not apply to truly irreversible decisions (e.g., fatal financial ruin, legal liability) — speaker context implies recoverable business errors

examples.text: Greg LaVecchia reflects on his own past mistakes at Bloom Nutrition, describing them as feeling like 'world-ending colossal mistakes, catastrophic mistakes' at the time. In retrospect, he identifies them as some of the cheapest lessons he could have bought — illustrating how the emotional experience of a mistake dramatically overstates its actual informational cost.

practices.text: Make fast decisions and improve in real time rather than waiting for perfect conditions or complete information before acting.
